chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Greeks: Reading an Option's Sensitivities

lessons.title: Delta and Gamma: How Price Moves With the Underlying

children.text: Delta has been in this course since Lesson 1.3, as the number of shares needed to replicate an option by hand, and Lesson 3.2 revealed it in closed form: a call's delta is exactly N(d1).

body.caption: A call's delta always sits between 0 and 1. A put's delta always sits between −1 and 0, exactly 1 lower than the call's, at the same strike and expiry.

children.text: Read delta as a local exchange rate: how many rupees the option's price moves for a ₹1 move in the underlying, right now. A call with delta 0.56 gains roughly 56 paise for every ₹1 rise in Nifty, for a small move. That word "local" matters, and the rest of this lesson is about exactly why.

body.text: It is tempting to call delta "the probability the option finishes in the money", and traders say this casually all the time. Be precise: Lesson 3.2 showed that N(d2), not N(d1), is the actual risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money. Delta, N(d1), is the weight on the stock-received term, not that probability. The two numbers are usually close, especially near the money where d1 and d2 sit near each other, which is exactly why the shorthand persists, but they are not the same quantity.

children.text: Delta Across the Chain: Revisiting Moneyness
Reuse Lesson 3.3's exact world (Nifty at 24,800, r = 6.5%, σ = 13%, one month to expiry) and compute delta across the same strike ladder Lesson 1.2 first introduced.

body.caption: Call delta across strikes, same inputs as Lesson 3.3

children.text: Delta falls smoothly from near 1 deep in the money to near 0 deep out of the money, exactly the reliability-versus-leverage picture Lesson 1.2 described in words: a deep ITM call moves almost rupee for rupee with Nifty (delta close to 1), while a deep OTM call barely reacts to an ordinary move (delta close to 0). Delta is that same intuition, now with an exact number attached.
Delta Hedging: Chapter 1's Replication, Now Named

Lesson 1.3 built a portfolio of 0.5 Reliance shares to hedge one call, without ever calling it by name. That was delta hedging: holding delta shares of the underlying against an options position so that, for a small move in either direction, the gain or loss on the shares offsets the gain or loss on the option. A market maker who sells options all day does exactly this, continuously, on a much larger scale, to earn the premium and time decay without taking on a directional bet on Nifty.

body.title: A market maker's hedge
body.scenario: A market maker sells 100 lots of the 24,800 ATM Nifty call from Lesson 3.3, with a delta of 0.5648. To hedge, she buys Nifty futures equivalent to 0.5648 × 100 lots worth of the underlying.
body.prompt: Nifty then rises by 50 points. Using only delta, roughly how will the gain or loss on her futures hedge compare to the loss on her short call position, and why is this hedge only approximately correct?
body.modelAnswer: Her short call position loses roughly delta × the move, about 0.5648 × 50 ≈ 28.24 points worth of value per lot, since she is short a call that gains value as Nifty rises. Her long futures hedge, sized at exactly that same delta, gains almost exactly that same amount as Nifty rises 50 points, so the two roughly offset and she is close to flat overall. The hedge is only approximate because delta itself is not constant: as Nifty moves, delta moves too, which is precisely what this lesson's next section, gamma, measures. A hedge built on today's delta drifts out of position as spot moves away from where it was set, which is why real hedgers rebalance repeatedly rather than hedging once and walking away.

children.text: Gamma: The Rate Delta Itself Changes

If delta is how fast the option's price moves with the underlying, gamma is how fast delta itself moves with the underlying, the option price's second derivative with respect to spot. Calls and puts at the same strike and expiry share an identical gamma, since a put's delta is always the call's delta minus exactly 1, a constant offset that vanishes the moment you look at the rate of change.

body.caption: φ(d1) is the standard normal probability density at d1, not N(d1). It is tallest at d1 = 0 and tapers off symmetrically on either side, which is exactly the shape gamma inherits.

children.text: For Lesson 3.3's exact ATM call, φ(d1) ≈ 0.3937, and S0 σ √T ≈ 24,800 × 0.13 × 0.28868 ≈ 930.69. That gives Γ ≈ 0.3937 ÷ 930.69 ≈ 0.000423 per rupee of Nifty movement, which reads more naturally scaled up: about 0.042 per 100-point move. In other words, a 100-point rise in Nifty would push this call's delta from about 0.5648 up to roughly 0.607, purely from gamma.

body.title: Illustrative gamma across strikes (per 100-point move in Nifty)

children.text: Gamma is highest for strikes close to the money and fades on both sides toward deep ITM and deep OTM, the same hump shape Lesson 1.2 found for time value. That is not a coincidence: both quantities are driven by the same thing, how much genuine uncertainty is left in whether the option finishes in or out of the money, which peaks right around the strike closest to spot.

body.text: High gamma is exactly why the market maker's scenario above needed rebalancing. Near the money, delta itself moves fast as spot moves, so a hedge set once quickly goes stale. Far from the money, gamma is low, delta barely moves, and the same hedge stays roughly correct for much longer. This is why options desks talk about "gamma risk" specifically around at-the-money positions close to expiry, where gamma is at its sharpest.

body.title: Delta or gamma?
body.question: A trader says, "My position's value barely reacts to a small Nifty move today, but that sensitivity itself is changing fast as Nifty drifts." Which Greek is doing the most work in the second half of that sentence?
options: Delta, because it measures sensitivity to the underlying
Gamma, because it measures how fast that sensitivity itself changes
Both describe exactly the same thing
body.explanation: The first half ("barely reacts to a small move") is a statement about delta, low right now. The second half ("that sensitivity itself is changing fast") is specifically what gamma measures: the rate of change of delta.

body.title: Project the new delta
body.prompt: Using this lesson's ATM figures (delta ≈ 0.5648, gamma ≈ 0.000423 per rupee), estimate the new delta if Nifty rises by 200 points.
body.explanation: New delta ≈ old delta + gamma × move = 0.5648 + (0.000423 × 200) = 0.5648 + 0.0846 ≈ 0.649. This is only a local approximation; gamma itself would also shift a little over such a large move.

body.text: Delta tells you how exposed you are to the underlying right now. Gamma tells you how quickly that exposure itself is about to change. A hedge that ignores gamma is only ever correct for an instant.

points: A call's delta is N(d1), between 0 and 1; a put's delta is N(d1) − 1, between −1 and 0.
Delta is not exactly the probability of finishing in the money (that is N(d2)), though the two are close near the money, which is why traders use delta as a rough proxy.
Delta hedging is Lesson 1.3's replicating-portfolio argument under its real name: holding delta shares (or futures) against an option to offset small moves in the underlying.
Gamma is the rate of change of delta, identical for a call and put at the same strike and expiry, and it peaks for strikes close to the money, the same hump shape Lesson 1.2 found for time value.
High gamma means a delta hedge goes stale quickly and needs frequent rebalancing; low gamma, typically deep ITM or deep OTM, means the same hedge stays roughly accurate for longer.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. All strikes, deltas, gammas, and the market maker's scenario are hypothetical, built on the same illustrative inputs as Lesson 3.3, not live market data.
